extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, and students seeking guidance on English grammar and word usage
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for correct word choice, grammar, and idiom in formal written English, with examples of common confusions, preferred forms, and cautions about jargon and verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: emotive; emotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish emotive (arousing intense feeling) from emotional (of, relating to, or involving intense feelings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use emotive when meaning 'arousing intense feeling' (e.g., emotive language calculated to persuade the jury); use emotional to describe states or responses (e.g., an emotional response).

rubrics_metrics.name: empathy; sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Empathy = the ability to understand others' feelings; sympathy = compassion or sorrow for another's misfortune (and can also mean support or mutual understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empathy for understanding others' feelings (e.g., tremendous empathy with others); sympathy for compassion or occasional support (e.g., our sympathies are with you).

rubrics_metrics.name: endemic
rubrics_metrics.description: See epidemic — endemic describes a disease being perennially present within a region or population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endemic describes a disease within a population (e.g., malaria is endemic in parts of Africa); avoid saying a region is endemic for a disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: endorse
rubrics_metrics.description: See approve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use endorse in contexts akin to approve; no extended guidance in this entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: enervate; innervate
rubrics_metrics.description: Enervate = to weaken or drain of energy. Innervate = to stimulate or provide with energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are antonyms—do not confuse draining of energy (enervate) with stimulating (innervate).

rubrics_metrics.name: enormity; enormousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Enormity = monstrousness or moral outrageousness; enormousness = hugeness or immensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use enormity for morally outrageous acts (e.g., the enormity of the Khmer Rouge’s killings) and enormousness for physical hugeness (e.g., the enormousness of Alaska).

rubrics_metrics.name: enough
rubrics_metrics.description: See adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry cross-references use of adequate; no extended guidance here.

rubrics_metrics.name: enquire
rubrics_metrics.description: See inquire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes British variants: enquire/enquiry primarily British; inquire/inquiry standard in American English.

rubrics_metrics.name: ensure; insure; assure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure = to make sure something will happen; insure = to underwrite financial risk; assure = to tell someone something to allay doubts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure events/occurrences, insure things (financial coverage), and assure people (reassurance).

rubrics_metrics.name: enthused (adj.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid enthused as an adjective; use enthusiastic instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer enthusiastic over enthused for adjectival use.

rubrics_metrics.name: enumerable; innumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerable = countable and listable. Innumerable = cannot practically be counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use enumerable for countable lists (e.g., the enumerable issues that we need on the agenda); innumerable for vast, uncountable quantities (e.g., innumerable stars). Beware similar pronunciation in speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: envy
rubrics_metrics.description: See jealousy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry cross-reference; jealousy discussed elsewhere as distinct from envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: epidemic; endemic; pandemic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epidemic = outbreak and spread through a limited area then subsides; endemic = perennially present in a region/population; pandemic = prevalent over a large area (nation, continent, or world).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use epidemic for localized outbreaks, endemic to describe disease presence (not regions), and pandemic for widespread global or continental prevalence (e.g., 1918-19 flu pandemic).

rubrics_metrics.name: equally as
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically faulty phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delete 'as' (use 'equally' rather than 'equally as').

rubrics_metrics.name: et al.
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviated form of et alii ('and others')—refers to people, not things; period required after 'al.' but not after 'et'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use et al. for people; remember punctuation rules. Cf. ete.

rubrics_metrics.name: etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviated form of et cetera ('and other things'); should not refer to people; implies a list is too extensive to recite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid etc. for people, avoid redundant uses (e.g., 'and etc.'), and avoid using it after 'for example' or similar phrases that should introduce a short list of examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: event (in the event that)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In the event that' is verbose/formal; equivalent to 'if'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'if' for clarity and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: eventuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Often displaces more specific everyday words like event, result, possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific words (event, result, possibility) over eventuality where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: every day (adv.) vs. everyday (adj.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every day (two words) is adverbial; everyday (one word) is adjectival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: 'wear your everyday clothes every day.'

rubrics_metrics.name: every one; everyone
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-word 'every one' = emphatic 'each'; 'everyone' = pronoun equivalent to everybody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'every one of them' for emphasis; use 'everyone' as a pronoun.

rubrics_metrics.name: everywhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'everywhere' over 'everyplace'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'everywhere' in standard usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: evoke; invoke
rubrics_metrics.description: Evoke = bring out or bring to mind. Invoke = assert as authority, appeal for help, or conjure up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evoke for eliciting memories or emotions (e.g., evoke laughter); invoke for appeals to authority or conjuring (e.g., invoke the Monroe Doctrine).

rubrics_metrics.name: exceptional; exceptionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional = uncommon, superior, rare. Exceptionable = objectionable or offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse praising (exceptional) with condemning (exceptionable).

rubrics_metrics.name: executor; administrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Executor = person designated in a will to distribute estate. Administrator = court-appointed person when no executor is named or no will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid feminine forms administratrix/executrix; unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: explicit; implicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit = deliberately and clearly spelled out. Implicit = not specifically stated but suggested or necessary to effectuate purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'implicit' to mean 'complete' or 'unmitigated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: the fact that
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrase is often maligned and can be avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hunt for a substitute before retaining 'the fact that'; sometimes replacing the phrase suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: farther; further
rubrics_metrics.description: Farther = physical distance. Further = figurative distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'farther' for physical travel (e.g., drove farther north) and 'further' for figurative sense (e.g., examine this further); it's a refinement appreciated by connoisseurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: faze; phase (vb.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faze = disturb or disconcert. Phase = schedule or perform in stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'faze' for emotional impact (Jones isn't fazed). Use 'phase in/out' for staged implementation; negative adjective 'unfazed' not 'unphased.'

rubrics_metrics.name: feel (verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak when used as substitute for 'think' or 'believe'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'think' or 'believe' where appropriate to avoid weak phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: feel bad
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'feel bad' (not 'feel badly') when the meaning is emotional state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See grammar entry 5.170 (not included here) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: fewer vs. less
rubrics_metrics.description: See less — fewer reserved for plural count nouns; less for singular mass nouns or amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'fewer calories' but 'less salt'; reserve fewer for plural count nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: fictional; fictitious; fictive
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional = relating to fiction as genre. Fictitious = imaginary/counterfeit/false. Fictive = possessing imaginative creation talent or synonym for fictional but often needless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the most precise term; note anthropological 'fictive kin.'

rubrics_metrics.name: finalize
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'to bring to an end or finish the last part of' and is associated with inflated jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'finish' when possible to avoid jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: first (enumerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations prefer first, second, third, etc.; avoid -ly forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'first, second, third' rather than 'firstly, secondly...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: fit (conjugation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally fit-fitted-fitted; contemporary American use fit-fit-fit is prevalent; passive voice often 'fitted'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept changing usage; note passive 'fitted' still normal (e.g., the horse was fitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: flagrant
rubrics_metrics.description: See blatant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to blatant.

rubrics_metrics.name: flair; flare (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flare = unsteady light or sudden outburst. Flair = outstanding talent or originality/stylishness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'flare' for light/outbursts (e.g., emergency flare); 'flair' for talent (e.g., a flair for mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: flammable; inflammable
rubrics_metrics.description: Flammable invented as alternative to inflammable which some misread as 'not combustible'; flammable is standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'flammable'; antonym is 'nonflammable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: flaunt; flout
rubrics_metrics.description: Flaunt = show off ostentatiously. Flout = openly disobey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the two (e.g., they flaunted their wealth vs. they flouted the rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: flounder; founder
rubrics_metrics.description: Flounder = struggle awkwardly. Founder = sink or run aground (literal of a boat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although figurative senses overlap, use images appropriately (e.g., the unprepared student floundered; the ship foundered).

rubrics_metrics.name: following (avoid for 'after')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'following' as an equivalent of 'after' because of potential miscue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'after' for clarity (e.g., After the presentation ... rather than Following the presentation ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: forbear (vb.) vs. forebear (n.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forbear = to refrain. Forebear = ancestor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spellings differ; do not confuse meanings; provide conjugation for forbear (forbear-forbore-forborne).

rubrics_metrics.name: forego; forgo
rubrics_metrics.description: Forego = to go before (as in foregoing paragraph). Forgo = to do without or renounce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forego in contexts like 'the foregoing paragraph' and forgo when meaning 'do without' (they decided to forgo that opportunity).

rubrics_metrics.name: foreword; preface
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreword = introductory essay written by someone other than the author. Preface = introductory essay by the book's author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms correctly; note spelling 'foreword' not 'forward' in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: former; latter
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply to pairs: former = first of two; latter = second of two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when referring to two items only.

rubrics_metrics.name: fortuitous; fortunate
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortuitous = happening by chance (usually with a good result). Fortunate = lucky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't conflate fortuitous with fortunate; fortuitous historically means 'by chance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: forward(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: See toward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to toward for prepositional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: free rein
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct idiom is 'free rein' (not 'free reign').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'free rein' for unrestricted freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: fulsome (adj.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not preferably mean 'very full' but 'too much, excessive to point of being repulsive'; 'fulsome praise' can suggest insincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using fulsome to mean 'abundant'—it can imply excess or insincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: future, in the near
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'soon' or 'shortly' instead of the phrase 'in the near future'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise alternatives where rhythm and clarity permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: gauntlet; gantlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Etymologically different; gauntlet (glove) and gantlope (ordeal), but gauntlet has taken over both senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'throw down the gauntlet' and 'run the gauntlet' (gauntlet is standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Considered a vulgarism when used as synonym for 'man'; can be objectionable or patronizing in some usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautiously; be aware of objections to using it outside contexts implying refined/cultured meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: get
rubrics_metrics.description: Shunned by some as too casual but often more natural than obtain or procure; conjugated get-got-gotten (AmE) or get-got-got (BrE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable in many contexts (e.g., get a divorce); note ability to form passive-like constructions (get stolen).

rubrics_metrics.name: gibe; jibe; jive
rubrics_metrics.description: Gibe = biting insult or taunt. Jibe = to be in accord or agree. Jive = noun referring to swing music or misleading talk; verb to dance or mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose correct term by meaning (e.g., hurled gibes vs. didn't jibe with the judge's view).

rubrics_metrics.name: gild; guild
rubrics_metrics.description: Guild = organization; gild = to put a thin layer of gold (literal or figurative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the two; e.g., a guild of goldsmiths vs. to gild a picture frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: go (conjugation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugated go-went-gone; 'went' appears as past participle only in dialect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard conjugation; 'went' not used as past participle in standard English.

rubrics_metrics.name: gourmet; gourmand
rubrics_metrics.description: Gourmet = appreciates fine points of food/drink. Gourmand = tends toward gluttony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose based on nuance: appreciation vs. gluttony.

rubrics_metrics.name: graduate (vb.) vs. graduate from
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate (transitive) = grant a diploma. Graduate from = receive a diploma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A school can graduate a student; a student graduates from a school. Don't say a student graduates a school.

rubrics_metrics.name: grateful; gratified
rubrics_metrics.description: Grateful = thankful. Gratified = pleased, satisfied, or indulged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term matching the emotional nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: grisly; grizzly
rubrics_metrics.description: Grisly = gruesome or horrible. Grizzly = grayish or relating to the grizzly bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the gruesome (grisly) with the bear/color (grizzly).

rubrics_metrics.name: guild; gild
rubrics_metrics.description: Guild = organization; gild = to put gold on something (verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid confusion; note figurative 'gilding the lily.'

rubrics_metrics.name: hail; hale
rubrics_metrics.description: Hail = salute/greet/acclaim or noun for ice pellets. Hale = compel to go (verb) or adjective meaning healthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use based on meaning (e.g., hailed as the greatest vs. haled into court).

rubrics_metrics.name: half (of)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delete 'of' whenever possible (e.g., 'half the furniture'). Verb agreement: singular when followed by singular noun, plural when followed by plural noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe verb agreement: 'half the state is' vs. 'half the people are.'

rubrics_metrics.name: handful
rubrics_metrics.description: If handful applies to a mass noun use singular verb; if to a plural count noun use plural verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match verb to noun type (e.g., a handful of trouble is ahead vs. only a handful of walnut trees still line Main Street).

rubrics_metrics.name: hangar; hanger
rubrics_metrics.description: Hangar = building for aircraft. Hanger = clothes hanger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct spelling based on meaning (airplane hangars vs. clothes hangers).

rubrics_metrics.name: hanged; hung
rubrics_metrics.description: Hanged = past participle when referring to execution by hanging. Hung = past form for other senses or when death not intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'hanged' for judicial executions; use 'hung' for other senses (e.g., Abdul hung up his clothes).

rubrics_metrics.name: hanger
rubrics_metrics.description: See hangar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference: hanger (clothes) vs. hangar (aircraft building).

rubrics_metrics.name: harass; embarrass
rubrics_metrics.description: Harass has one 'r'; embarrass has two 'r's. Pronunciation varies between AmE and BrE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell correctly; be aware of pronunciation differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: harebrained
rubrics_metrics.description: Spelled 'harebrained' (not hairbrained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'hare' spelling derived from the timid animal.

rubrics_metrics.name: hark back
rubrics_metrics.description: So written—preferable to harken back or hearken back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'hark back'.

rubrics_metrics.name: healthy; healthful
rubrics_metrics.description: Healthy = enjoying good health. Healthful = promotes health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'a healthful diet' to mean promotes health; 'healthy' is taking over both senses but traditional distinction remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: help (to)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the 'to' when possible (e.g., talking will help resolve the problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concision by dropping unnecessary 'to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: he or she
rubrics_metrics.description: Used to avoid sexist 'he' generic; use sparingly and after other methods of gender neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer less obtrusive gender-neutral methods when possible; 'he or she' better than he/she, s/he, (s)he.

rubrics_metrics.name: historic; historical
rubrics_metrics.description: Historic = momentous in history. Historical = pertaining to or occurring in history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose based on nuance (e.g., a historic day vs. the historical record).

rubrics_metrics.name: hoard; horde
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoard = supply amassed (noun/verb). Horde = large crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'hoard' for secret/valuable supplies and 'horde' for noisy crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: hoi polloi
rubrics_metrics.description: Mildly disparaging phrase for 'common people'; is plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misuse to refer to elites; common phrase 'the hoi polloi' is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: holocaust
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalized = Nazi genocide of European Jews. Lowercase = extensive devastation by fire or systematic killings on a vast scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid light or hyperbolic uses of the word.

rubrics_metrics.name: home in
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct is 'home in' (not 'hone in'); means to come closer to a target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'hone' for 'sharpen'; use 'home in' for homing behavior or targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: homicide
rubrics_metrics.description: See murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to murder.

rubrics_metrics.name: hopefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Older meaning = 'in a hopeful manner'; newer sentence-adverb meaning = 'it is to be hoped that' or 'I hope', which is now accepted by many though some writers deplore it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of evolving usage; both meanings encountered—some careful writers still avoid the newer sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: humanitarian
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'involving promotion of human welfare'; avoid using it to mean simply 'human' (e.g., worst humanitarian disaster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'human' if that is the intended sense; 'humanitarian' implies welfare/promotion of welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: hung
rubrics_metrics.description: See hanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference about correct usage for execution vs. non-execution senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: I; me
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the appropriate first-person pronoun; be sure to pick the right one (e.g., Sally and I are planning to go vs. give John or me a call).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's not immodest to use I; ensure grammatical correctness like 'between you and me.'

rubrics_metrics.name: idyllic
rubrics_metrics.description: From 'idyll' meaning short pastoral poem; idyllic means charming or picturesque—not synonymous with ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'idyllic' for pastoral charm, not 'ideal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: i.e.; e.g.
rubrics_metrics.description: i.e. = id est ('that is'); e.g. = exempli gratia ('for example'). English equivalents are preferable in formal prose but the abbreviations are compact and sometimes desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always put a comma after either one in formal prose; see other sections for related punctuation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: if; whether
rubrics_metrics.description: If is conditional; whether introduces an alternative often in indirect questions. Use whether to introduce noun clauses or to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whether to introduce noun clauses (he asked whether his tie was straight) and when 'if' produces ambiguity; prefer whether in formal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: ilk
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly means 'type' or 'sort' in modern usage; Scottish phrase 'of that ilk' has a different meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'of his ilk' or 'of that ilk' correctly; note modern acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: illegal
rubrics_metrics.description: See unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: illegible; unreadable
rubrics_metrics.description: Illegible = handwriting or printing not clear enough to be read. Unreadable = so poorly composed as to be incomprehensible or intolerably dull.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish legibility from literary quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: illicit
rubrics_metrics.description: See elicit; unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to related words.

rubrics_metrics.name: illude
rubrics_metrics.description: See allude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference—avoid confusion with 'allude.'

rubrics_metrics.name: immigrate; emigrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Immigrate = enter a country to live permanently. Emigrate = leave one country to live in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perspective matters: one is an immigrant here and an emigrant there; émigré often implies political exile.

rubrics_metrics.name: imminent
rubrics_metrics.description: See eminent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference; do not confuse 'imminent' (about to happen) with 'eminent' (distinguished).

rubrics_metrics.name: impact; impactful
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist using 'impact' as a verb; 'impactful' is jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'affect' or 'influence' instead of 'impact' (verb); replace 'impactful' with 'influential' or 'powerful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative equivalent of an indictment, not a conviction; in US federal system House votes on impeachment and Senate votes on removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish impeachment (indictment-like) from conviction/removal; be precise in political/legal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: impelled
rubrics_metrics.description: See compelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to compelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: implicit
rubrics_metrics.description: See explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference and note not to misuse implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: imply; infer
rubrics_metrics.description: Writer/speaker implies; reader/listener infers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the two; avoid using 'infer' when 'imply' is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: important; importantly
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionalists prefer 'more important' (ellipsis) over 'more importantly' in initial phrase, but 'more importantly' as a sentence adverb is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms are in use; 'more importantly' is now unobjectionable in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: impractical; impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: Impractical = not sensible or unrealistic. Impracticable = impossible to carry out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'impracticable' for impossibility (e.g., landing on that hole-ridden runway proved impracticable).

rubrics_metrics.name: in actual fact
rubrics_metrics.description: See actual fact, in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference; prefer concise alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: inasmuch as
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'because' or 'since' in most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simpler alternatives unless a formal tone requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: in behalf of
rubrics_metrics.description: See behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: incidence; incident; instance
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidence = relative rates/ranges. Incident = event/occurrence. Instance = case/example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'incidence' for scientific/statistical contexts; use 'incident' for events and 'instance' for cases/examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: include; comprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Include implies nonexclusivity. Comprise implies exclusivity (the whole consists of the listed parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use include when the list is nonexclusive (the collection includes 126 portraits); use comprise when the list is exhaustive (the collection comprises 126 silver spoons). Note patent-law exception where 'comprise' can be nonexclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: in connection with
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague, fuzzy phrase meaning related to or associated with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more specific words like of, related to, associated with, about, or for to improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: incredible; incredulous
rubrics_metrics.description: Incredible = too strange to be believed (or colloquially 'astonishingly good'). Incredulous = disbelieving or skeptical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'incredible' with caution in figurative senses; choose 'incredulous' for skeptical attitude of people.

rubrics_metrics.name: inculcate; indoctrinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Inculcate = instill values into someone (take 'into' and a value). Indoctrinate = teach/brainwash people with values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'inculcate courage into soldiers' vs. 'indoctrinate children with the habit of telling the truth.' Note differences in object selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Use to distinguish a single person from a group; prefer more specific term (person, adult, child, man, woman) when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'individual' sparingly; prefer specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: induce
rubrics_metrics.description: See adduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: in excess of
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbose phrase; try replacing with 'more than' or 'over'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise alternatives like 'more than' or 'over.'

rubrics_metrics.name: infectious
rubrics_metrics.description: See contagious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: infer
rubrics_metrics.description: See imply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference; remind that infer is for readers deducing, not writers suggesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the verb 'draw' rather than 'make' with inference (they drew the wrong inferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'make' with 'inference' to prevent confusion with implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: inflammable
rubrics_metrics.description: See flammable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference; prefer 'flammable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: inflict; afflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflict = events/illnesses/punishments are inflicted on; afflicted = sufferers are afflicted with/by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'inflict cruelty on' vs. 'afflicted with drought.' Ensure correct verb-object relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: ingenious; ingenuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Ingenious = intelligent, clever, original. Ingenuous = candid, naive, without dissimulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse cleverness (ingenious) with naiveté/openness (ingenuous).

rubrics_metrics.name: innate; inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate = present from birth (usually living things). Inherent = part of a thing's nature (life not implied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose term according to whether life or birth is implicated (e.g., innate talent vs. inherent hardness of a rock).

rubrics_metrics.name: innervate
rubrics_metrics.description: See enervate (antonym).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference; innervate = stimulate/provide with energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: innocent; not guilty
rubrics_metrics.description: Innocent = without blame. Not guilty = exonerated by a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate moral innocence from legal verdict; newspapers avoid 'not guilty' due to risk of omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: innumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: See enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference: innumerable = cannot be counted; enumerable = countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: in order to; in order for
rubrics_metrics.description: Often reducible to 'to' and 'for' respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the shorter 'to' or 'for' when rhythm and euphony permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: in proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: See close proximity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference; avoid verbose phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: inquire
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal American and British spellings are 'inquire' and 'inquiry'; 'enquire'/'enquiry' primarily British.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose spelling according to variety of English being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: in regard to
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrase 'in regard to' (not nonstandard 'in regards to'); prefer single-word substitutes like about, regarding, concerning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise alternatives where possible for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: insidious; invidious
rubrics_metrics.description: Insidious = spreads gradually to cause damage without being noticed. Invidious = morally offensive or causing unpleasantness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the term matching the nuance (insidious conspiracy vs. invidious discrimination).

rubrics_metrics.name: in spite of
rubrics_metrics.description: See despite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'despite' in many contexts as more concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: instance
rubrics_metrics.description: See incidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to incidence/incident/instance distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: insure
rubrics_metrics.description: See ensure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference: 'insure' for underwriting financial risk; 'ensure' to make certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: intense; intensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Intense = having a strong effect/ involving great effort in short time/ having unduly strong feelings. Intensive = used in compounds (labor-intensive) or customary terms like intensive care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'intense' for general senses except customary uses of 'intensive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: intently; intensely
rubrics_metrics.description: Intently = purposefully with concentration. Intensely = with great power, passion, or emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish deliberate focus (intently) from intensity of feeling or power (intensely).

rubrics_metrics.name: inter; intern
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter = to bury. Intern (noun) = student working temporarily; intern (verb) = to work as an intern or to confine civilians without charge in wartime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of both noun and dual-verb senses of 'intern' and the distinct meaning of 'inter' (bury).

rubrics_metrics.name: in the affirmative / in the negative
rubrics_metrics.description: See affirmative, in the.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference for usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: inveigh; inveigle
rubrics_metrics.description: Inveigh = protest (usually against). Inveigle = cajole or ensnare, often by misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose verb according to action: protest vs. cajole/ensnare.

rubrics_metrics.name: invoke
rubrics_metrics.description: See evoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference: invoke has senses including appeal to authority, conjuring, etc.; evoke brings out or to mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: irregardless
rubrics_metrics.description: An error; use regardless (or possibly irrespective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'irregardless' as nonstandard.

rubrics_metrics.name: it is I; it is me
rubrics_metrics.description: Both are correct; 'it is I' is strictly grammatical and stuffy; 'it is me' is idiomatic and relaxed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both acceptable in modern usage though stricter contexts may prefer 'it is I.' In third-person constructions, maintain greater stringency ('this is he').

rubrics_metrics.name: its; it's
rubrics_metrics.description: Its = possessive form of it. It's = contraction of 'it is'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correctly to avoid possessive vs. contraction errors (e.g., it's a sad dog that scratches its fleas).

rubrics_metrics.name: jealousy; envy
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy = resentment toward another (especially in intimate relationships). Envy = coveting another's advantages, possessions, or abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms to match emotional nuance (sexual jealousy vs. envy of success).

rubrics_metrics.name: jibe; jive
rubrics_metrics.description: See gibe/jibe/jive distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference: jibe = agree/accord; jive = dance/music or misleading talk; gibe = taunt.

rubrics_metrics.name: karat
rubrics_metrics.description: See carat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference differences in measurement terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: kudos
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'praise and admiration'; singular (not plural); pronounce /k[y]oo-dos/ preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'kudo is' or 'kudos are'; treat the word as singular.

rubrics_metrics.name: lady
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'lady' as synonym for 'woman' can be objectionable/patronizing in some contexts, especially for unprestigious jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautiously; be aware of potential offense (e.g., cleaning lady). Cf. gentleman.

rubrics_metrics.name: last; lastly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'last' when introducing final point in a list (consistent with first, second, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'last' or 'finally' rather than 'lastly' to match style of enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: laudable; laudatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laudable = praiseworthy even if not fully successful. Laudatory = expressing praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'laudable effort' vs. 'laudatory phone calls' appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: lay; lie
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay = transitive verb (requires direct object) inflected lay-laid-laid. Lie = intransitive verb inflected lie-lay-lain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lay when object present (lay your pencils down). Use lie for reclining (lie down). Use mnemonic 'Now I lay me down to sleep.'

rubrics_metrics.name: leach; leech
rubrics_metrics.description: Leach = to percolate/separate solids in solution. Leech = bloodsucker; as verb, to attach or drain resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct spelling/meaning depending on context (chemical process vs. parasitic/figurative draining).

rubrics_metrics.name: lead
rubrics_metrics.description: See led.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference correct past tense 'led' vs. metal 'lead' confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: lease; let
rubrics_metrics.description: Lease and let both valid; let is older than lease. Distinction: either owner or tenant can lease property, but only owner can let it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms correctly based on agency (owner vs. tenant).

rubrics_metrics.name: led
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct past tense and past participle of 'lead' is 'led'; often misspelled as 'lead'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'led' appropriately; watch for confusion with metal 'lead' pronunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: lend (vb.) vs. loan (vb. & n.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lend = letting someone use something to be returned. Loan = verb particularly with money but lend appears more in edited English; 'loan' is noun corresponding to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past tense of 'lend' is 'lent'; choose verb/noun form appropriately (lend vs. loan).

rubrics_metrics.name: less; fewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Less reserved for singular mass nouns/amounts; fewer for plural count nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'less salt' vs. 'fewer calories'; plural verb agreement rules often follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: lest
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually calls for subjunctive verb; somewhat more common in British English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with subjunctive (he didn't want to drive lest he take a wrong turn).

rubrics_metrics.name: let
rubrics_metrics.description: See lease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference usage distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: libel
rubrics_metrics.description: See defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference legal terminology distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: lie
rubrics_metrics.description: See lay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference conjugation and transitivity distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: life-and-death; life-or-death
rubrics_metrics.description: Life-and-death is standard idiom (despite logical issue of mutual exclusivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'life-and-death decision' as standard phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: light (verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verb inflections: light-lit-lit or light-lighted-lighted acceptable. Past-participial adjective tends to be 'lighted' when not modified by -ly adverb, 'lit' if preceded by -ly adverb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., a lighted building vs. brightly lit sconces; both forms acceptable with nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: like; as
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally 'like' is a preposition and 'as' a conjunction; 'like' as conjunction is casual but increasingly common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'as' or 'as if' in Standard Written English for conjunctive senses to avoid provoking frowns; 'like' as conjunction acceptable in casual contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: literally
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'actually; without exaggeration' and should not be used loosely in figurative senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid figurative misuse (e.g., they were literally glued to their seats) unless literal meaning is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: loathe (vb.); loath (adj.)
rubrics_metrics.description: To loathe = detest intensely. Loath (adj.) = reluctant or unwilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation differs ('loath' with th of 'thing'); use correct form for meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: lose; loose; loosen
rubrics_metrics.description: Lose = be deprived. Loose = release or set free (verb) or adjective meaning not tight. Loosen = make less tight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the three to avoid error (e.g., lose vs. loose vs. loosen).

rubrics_metrics.name: luxuriant; luxurious
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxuriant = lush and grows abundantly. Luxurious = lavish, extravagant, comfortable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use based on sense (e.g., luxuriant head of hair vs. luxurious resort).

rubrics_metrics.name: mad; angry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mad meaning angry dates back centuries but is stigmatized in formal writing; many avoid it in formal contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'angry' in formal writing though 'mad' is common in everyday use.

rubrics_metrics.name: majority
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferably denotes countable things; when referring to preponderance of votes majority takes singular verb, but when referring to predominant group of people or things it can take singular or plural verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'most' where it fits; observe verb agreement rules depending on noun/phrase following majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: malevolent; maleficent
rubrics_metrics.description: Malevolent = evil mind wishing to harm. Maleficent = desire by miscreant to accomplish evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the term matching nuance of malevolence or active malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: malodorous
rubrics_metrics.description: See odious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: maltreatment
rubrics_metrics.description: See mistreatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference; maltreatment often denotes harsher abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using 'humankind' instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gender-neutral alternatives where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: manslaughter
rubrics_metrics.description: See murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference legal terminology differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: mantle; mantel
rubrics_metrics.description: Mantle = long, loose garment or metaphorical covering. Mantel = structure around a fireplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct spelling per meaning (e.g., assuming the mantle of a martyr vs. family pictures on the mantel).

rubrics_metrics.name: masterful; masterly
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterful = dominating and imperious. Masterly = having mastered a craft; authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'masterly' for skilled, authoritative work (e.g., a masterly analysis); consider phrasing for adverb (in a masterly way).

rubrics_metrics.name: may; can
rubrics_metrics.description: See can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference modal verb distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: may; might
rubrics_metrics.description: May = expresses possibility or factual possibility. Might = suggests uncertainty, hypothetical, or contrary-to-fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'may' when something is possible or factual (I may have turned off the stove); use 'might' for hypothetical or counterfactual (I might have won if ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: medal; meddle; metal; mettle
rubrics_metrics.description: Medal = award. Meddle = interfere. Metal = substance. Mettle = character/courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose correct word by meaning; watch homophones.

rubrics_metrics.name: media; mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural of medium in scientific or mass-communications contexts is 'media'. For spiritualists, plural is 'mediums'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'the media are' (plural) in journalistic contexts; use 'mediums' for spiritual mediums.

rubrics_metrics.name: memoranda; memorandums
rubrics_metrics.description: Both plural forms correct; memoranda has predominated since early 19th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use 'memoranda' as singular; e.g., this memorandum is / these memoranda are.

rubrics_metrics.name: mete out
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct phrase meaning 'to distribute' or 'assign' is 'mete out'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the erroneous 'meet out' and wrong past tense 'meeted out'.

rubrics_metrics.name: might
rubrics_metrics.description: See may.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference modal usage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: militate
rubrics_metrics.description: See mitigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference similar-sounding verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: minuscule
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'very small'; commonly misspelled 'miniscule'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct spelling 'minuscule'; note printing sense of minuscules (lowercase).

rubrics_metrics.name: mistreatment; maltreatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistreatment = general term. Maltreatment = harsh form involving abuse by rough/cruel handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the term matching severity of abuse.
